editorNote: Adventure writers rethink puzzles while the home computer reaches outward through the telephone and toward the living room.
morningLine: Amazon puts cleverness first; Wozniak sets his sights beyond the computer.

lead.headline: Michael Crichton wants adventure games to make sense
body: Michael Crichton has a complaint familiar to anyone stranded at an adventure-game prompt: a sensible solution ought not to fail merely because the player has guessed the wrong words. In February’s COMPUTE!, the novelist discusses Amazon and argues for puzzles that answer to the logic of the situation rather than an arbitrary phrase.

His damaged boat offers an example. Players can patch it in three plausible ways, an invitation to think through the problem rather than hunt for a single approved command. Crichton favors cleverness over violence and has little affection for mazes. The interview treats the adventure as an existing game, not a new release this week.

The project began with scripting in 1982. Crichton knew BASIC, but brought in Steve Warrady to help realize the story in Apple assembly-language graphics and text. Development took about eighteen months, with writer, programmer and graphic designer working in a collaboration he compares to a film crew.

Trillium approached him about adventures based on novels while he was polishing Amazon. The timing was a coincidence: he already had a game under way. For home-computer players, the interesting promise is not simply a famous name on a box, but a story world that rewards a reasonable idea.
lead.dek: February’s COMPUTE! finds the novelist building adventures around believable solutions, not magic words.

stories.headline: Wozniak leaves daily Apple duties for a living-room video venture
body: Apple co-founder Stephen Wozniak is giving up his daily principal-engineer duties to pursue a self-financed business involving video in the living room. Kathleen Day’s February 7 Los Angeles Times report says Apple confirmed the change Wednesday, after employees were told in a Tuesday newsletter.

This is not a complete break with Apple. Wozniak remains on the payroll as a consultant. Joe Ennis, another key Apple engineer, is leaving with him, giving the new undertaking a second experienced designer.

Wozniak is withholding product details and hopes to have something ready by the fall. No price or technical specifications have been disclosed. The Apple II designer’s next direction is intriguing, but a proposed home-video business is not yet a product on the dealer’s shelf.

stories.headline: Online games and conversation challenge the established services
body: An evening online need not mean only messages or stock tables. February’s Telecomputing Today column in COMPUTE! describes Play/Net’s medium-resolution color games for the Commodore 64, reached with a proprietary terminal program at an introductory $2 an hour.

People/Link is courting callers at an introductory $2.95 an hour with conversation, special-interest activities and electronic mail. Its advertising names Partyline, Club-Link, Netmail and PeopleScan, as well as chess and bridge. These are connect-time offers, not a guarantee that every telephone or access charge is included.

Play/Net says IBM and Apple support will follow by spring; that remains a promise rather than present availability. Columnist Arlan R. Levitan also expects introductory prices to rise. The attraction is immediate nonetheless: the opponent or conversation partner can be at another keyboard.

stories.headline: PC-Write turns copying into a sales channel
body: Quicksoft’s PC-Write makes distribution part of the sales pitch. Sheldon Leemon’s February COMPUTE! review encourages owners to pass the word processor and its documentation to friends, user groups and bulletin boards. This is authorized sharing, not illicit copying.

Bob Wallace, formerly of Microsoft, designed the program. A $75 registration buys a personalized copy, bound manual, assistance, Pascal and machine-language source, and the next major update. When a personalized copy produces another registration, its owner receives $25.

The practical tools include search and replace, recoverable deletions, adjustable margins, help screens and macros, with special handling for the PCjr keyboard. Editing and printing are separate programs. Buyers should note a discrepancy in the review: its body quotes $10 for disk and postage, while the closing product box lists $20 for the program disk.

briefs.headline: BBS advice beats the hotel booklet
briefs.summary: Levitan reports asking an unnamed local San Francisco BBS for restaurant recommendations while traveling, then enjoying Szechwan food based on a reply. Do not invent the board name or turn the account into a newly dated February event.

briefs.headline: Electronic airline searching
briefs.summary: Levitan says an Official Airline Guide search took about 90 seconds and cost roughly $1.50. A separate CompuServe/TWA Travelshopper advertisement says customers can inspect flight availability and order tickets; distinguish these different offerings.

worldAnchor.headline: New Zealand’s nuclear stance puts ANZUS under strain
worldAnchor.summary: New Zealand’s rejection of a USS Buchanan visit has put the ANZUS alliance under strain. A February 6 report describes cancellation of next month’s Sea Eagle exercises and an alliance review, as David Lange maintains his policy is directed at nuclear weapons rather than the United States.

bbsNote.headline: At $2 an hour, online play joins a busy dial-up marketplace
bbsNote.summary: February COMPUTE! supplies dated coverage of online games, chat, stock information, portable telecommuting and a new terminal listing. The posts below are research summaries, not fabricated historical BBS messages.

posts.text: Introductory $2/hour color online games; proprietary terminal program; IBM and Apple support only promised for spring.
Introductory $2.95/hour; Partyline public/private live conversation, Club-Link interest groups, Netmail and PeopleScan advertised.
Plus/Term supports up to 1200 bps, file transfers, key redefinition and word wrapping; VIC needs at least 16K RAM. No modem purchase price established.
Levitan’s travel column recounts requesting local restaurant tips; no named sysop or board in the account.
Last-trade quote surcharges $12/month and $20/month respectively, on top of connect time; Source/Spears online trading described as a service, not a consumer how-to.

curiosity.headline: The word processor that pays you to give it away
curiosity.summary: PC-Write’s registered users can earn $25 each time a shared copy produces a new $75 registration.
curiosity.detail: COMPUTE!’s February review calls the referral system the software equivalent of a legal chain letter. Authorized copying is central to Quicksoft’s business model; this is not a piracy report. The review’s separate disk-only prices conflict ($10 in the body; $20 in its product box).

gadgetWatch.headline: Apple founder aims at the living room
gadgetWatch.summary: Wozniak’s new self-financed home-video business is announced this week, with Joe Ennis joining him and an autumn product target. The February 7 contemporary report gives no product name, price or specifications; do not call the eventual CL 9 remote control a shipped 1985 product.

market.headline: Commodore’s inventory hangover lingers
market.summary: February 1 reporting provides the backdrop: quarterly profit fell 94 percent to $3.2 million, sales declined 21 percent to $338.7 million, and inventory stood near $400 million. Analyst forecasts for cheaper C64s and a forthcoming Amiga are not confirmed shelf offers.
